column3: Replays harm, calling, a granted favor, and the recipient's false self-attribution.
Rejects calling on alternatives unable to cause benefit or harm.
Pairs brief worldly enjoyment with the final destination of Hell.
Closely repeats harm, return to the Lord, mercy, then renewed association.
The near context contrasts the focus's defiance with fear of the great punishment.
Forgetting God provides a broader pattern of reciprocal abandonment and wrongdoing.
Closely parallels harm-driven calling followed by passing on after relief.
Shows an enduring call to the Lord under bodily harm, without the later relapse.
Directly joins rivals, diversion from God's path, brief enjoyment, and the Fire.
Contrasts withdrawal in ease with despair when harm touches a person.
Supplies the merciful removal of harm that the focus treats as a test of fidelity.
States that brief enjoyment is followed by compelled exposure to severe punishment.
Shows a person misconstruing bestowed ease as proof of personal honor.
The immediate contrast presents sustained worship, fear, and hope instead of crisis-only return.
Closely matches mercy after hardship being claimed as personal entitlement and followed by judgment.
Links removed mercy with human despair and ingratitude, but reverses the focus's sequence.
Replays distress, exclusive calling, rescue, and subsequent turning away.
Denies that alternative protectors can help or supply a path apart from God.
Connects arrogant turning with leading others away from God's path and final punishment.
The near appeal to God's judgment frames the ultimate resolution of the focus's divided claims.
Clarifies the focus's brief enjoyment against the lasting scale of the Hereafter.
Depicts imposed disbelief and the making of rivals as a cause of later regret.
The near reminder theme opposes the forgetfulness displayed in the focus.
Its servant who turns to God offers only a limited contrast to the focus's return.
Links a small worldly price with obstructing God's path.
Provides a faithful exemplar of turning to God, without the focus's trial-and-relapse cycle.
The gathering of God's enemies to the Fire adds no distinct route to the focus.
Explicitly pairs limited enjoyment for disbelief with being driven to the Fire.
Challenges the efficacy of intercessors, sharpening the focus's made rivals.
Connects ingratitude for what was given with temporary enjoyment and coming knowledge.
Shows an alternative discourse used to lead people away from God's path.
Its catalogue of persevering devotion offers a broad contrast to unstable return.
Directly challenges making rivals for the Creator and Lord of all worlds.
Exposes rivals as objects of misplaced devotion before the reality of divine power and punishment.
The immediate declaration of submission provides only a general contrast to association.
Directly connects disbelief in bestowed gifts with the command to enjoy temporarily.
Names the adversarial call that leads people toward becoming companions of the Blaze.
Models persistent devotion and remembrance rather than the focus's conditional return.
The promise that the messenger will not forget does not clarify human forgetfulness after relief.
The dispute over following for spoils lacks a material connection to the focus.
The near contrast of opened and hardened hearts only broadly frames guidance and error.
The origin of jinn from fire does not clarify the focus's moral sequence.
Denies the efficacy of what is called besides God and names the transgressors as companions of Fire.
The question about former generations adds no route to the focus.
Shows bestowed possessions left behind and claimed partners absent at final return.
Its legal contrast and mention of Fire do not materially clarify crisis, rivals, or ingratitude.
The near portrayal of disbelievers entering Hell develops the focus's closing warning.
The defeat of an invading plan has no usable link to the focus's themes.
A righteous supplication supplies only the general act of calling the Lord.
Crisis at sea concentrates worship in a sincere call for rescue.
Denies that self-made gods can avert harm or rescue when the Merciful wills it.
Forgetting the fish and its path in the sea is unrelated to the focus.
The near assertion of God's oneness and overpowering rule counters all rival attribution.
Links limited worldly concern with losing the path of guidance.
Grounds the prohibition of making rivals in the Creator's provision of the world.
God's merciful forbearance offers only a distant frame for the focus's warning.
The brothers' charge of their father's error does not clarify the focus.
The gift of faculties and scarce gratitude broadly echoes the focus's ingratitude.
The reward of doers of good is only a general contrast to the focus's consequence.
Links divine guidance with those who repeatedly turn back to Him.
States that even mercy and removal of harm would leave some persisting in transgression.
Reasserts worship of God alone against refusal of the message.
Explicitly says every blessing is from God and that people cry to Him when harm strikes.
Its promise of Fire for disbelief is too general to clarify the focus's sequence.
The near reward for good works gives only a broad outcome contrast.
Tests granted security by exclusive worship and warns against association after it.
Joins obstructing God's path, disbelief, and the Fire as a final consequence.
The near claim that intermediaries bring nearness exposes a rival rationale for divided worship.
Its bare statement of disbelief and future knowledge adds little beyond the focus's warning.
Connects bestowed faculties with the scarcity of gratitude.
The near account of ordered creation supports the focus's rejection of competing divine claims.
The placement of moon and sun has no material route to the focus.
The fish taking a path through the sea is unrelated to the focus.
The near call not to despair invites return after the excess implied by the focus.
Names punishment by the Fire for disbelievers, extending the focus's final warning.
Portrays approach to God as an active path, contrasting diversion from His path.
The near declaration of divine lordship and sole divinity grounds the rejection of rivals.
Directly contrasts worldly enjoyment with return to God and severe punishment for disbelief.
Shows false attribution to God being used to lead people astray.
The immediate call to God-conscious endurance offers a durable alternative to short enjoyment.
Distinguishes being led astray by worshiped beings from losing the path oneself.
Creation followed by disbelievers equating others with their Lord directly counters rival-making.
The near rebuke for underestimating God culminates in transcendence above their associations.
Solomon's later return offers only a limited instance of turning back after trial.
Material provisions and temporary enjoyment only broadly resemble the focus's granted blessing.
The near warning of layers of Fire develops the consequence announced in the focus.
Dispute about the Hour and distant error only generally echo the focus's end warning.
The image of being driven into Hell reinforces the focus's announced destination.
The immediate prior ayah contrasts disbelief with gratitude and confirms return for full accounting.
Its general woe for disbelievers adds little beyond the focus's explicit Fire warning.
Giving little then withholding does not clarify the focus's sequence.
The distinction between combatants and those with disability is unrelated to the focus.
Inheritance allocations do not provide a route to the focus.
Connects worldly distraction and forgetting the final meeting with reciprocal abandonment.
Confession that the Lord is God offers only a broad contrast to associating rivals.
Links obstruction of God's path, its distortion, and denial of the Hereafter.
Treats misplaced loyalty as straying from the level path, but not the focus's crisis pattern.
Shows a changing condition being turned into persistent disbelief after prior favor.
Rules of household etiquette and purity do not clarify the focus.
Shows a community being led astray during a test, complementing the focus's diversion theme.
States that distress makes people call God alone, after which they forget their associates.
Depicts desperate calling to God for rescue from land and sea, with a pledge of gratitude.
Completes the rescue sequence by naming the return to association after deliverance.
Places adversity and hardship as conditions intended to prompt humility before God.
Shows hardship replaced with ease, followed by complacent misreading of the changed condition.
Directly portrays partners being ascribed to God after a granted blessing.
Connects mercy after harm with a renewed adverse response to God's signs.
Completes the sea-rescue scene with transgression after God has saved them.
Rejects worship of alternatives that can neither harm nor benefit and are called intercessors.
Closely matches favor after hardship being received with boastful, self-satisfied dismissal.
Directly states that, once harm is removed, some associate partners with their Lord.
Replays sincere calling in maritime danger followed by association after rescue on land.
Questions whether any authority supports the partners credited after mercy.
Shows overwhelming danger producing sincere devotion, while rescue exposes divided response.
Contrasts aversion to God alone with delight at mention of those associated with Him.
Contrasts a call to associate with God against the call to the Mighty, Forgiving God.
Closely repeats withdrawal under favor and abundant calling when harm touches a person.
Links assigning a share to God with human ingratitude toward the Creator.
Describes human instability between hardship and received good, without the focus's return or association.
Exposes the inverse error of treating restricted provision as proof of humiliation.
